opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think Meta still has a real shot, but it depends on what you mean by "winning." If the question is who has the single best model on a leaderboard at any given moment, that changes every few months, and nobody holds that position for long. Meta has had periods where it was clearly behind the frontier and periods where it was very close.

What Meta does have is a few structural advantages that are hard to replicate. First, compute. Very few companies can put that much hardware behind training runs, and the leadership has been willing to spend at a scale that signals they see this as existential, not optional. Second, distribution. Billions of people use Meta's products every day, so the moment you have a capable model, there's an enormous surface to deploy it on and learn from real usage. Third, there's a strong research culture with a long history in AI, going back to FAIR. A lot of foundational work came out of that environment.

The challenges are also real. Building frontier models is not only about compute and talent. It's about organization, how quickly you can iterate, how well research and product teams coordinate, and whether you make the right bets on data, architecture, and post-training. Large organizations can move slowly, and with so many people involved, decision-making gets complicated. In this field, a small team with a clear direction can sometimes move faster than a big team with lots of resources.

There's also the strategic question around open versus closed models. Releasing open weights earned Meta a lot of goodwill and a big developer ecosystem, but it's a difficult balance when you're also trying to stay at the frontier and justify massive investments.

So my overall view is that Meta is absolutely a serious contender, but the outcome will be decided less by resources, which they clearly have, and more by execution and whether they can keep the research side genuinely creative rather than just chasing what others have already done. In the long run, I think the people who find the next real idea, not just scale the current one, will have the biggest advantage.

r001.rationale: The candidate says leaderboard leaders change every few months and nobody holds that position for long, clearly communicating that there are no permanent winners.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I'm speaking for myself here, not for the company, so take this as one researcher's view.

I'd break it down into a few pieces, because "chances" really depends on what game you think is being played.

If the question is whether Meta can train a frontier-quality model, I think the answer is clearly yes. The ingredients are there: a very large compute footprint, a lot of data, and a research culture at FAIR and GenAI that has been doing this kind of work for a long time. Llama showed that we can go from fairly far behind to roughly on the frontier in a short period, and the training recipes, the data pipelines, the infrastructure for large distributed runs, all of that has matured a lot internally.

But I'd actually argue Meta isn't playing the same game as, say, OpenAI or Anthropic, and it shouldn't try to. Meta doesn't sell model access as its core business. Its business is products that a few billion people use. So the question that matters internally is less "do we have the single best model on a leaderboard this quarter" and more "can we make models good enough, cheap enough, and controllable enough to put into everything we build." That's a different optimization target. It favors efficiency, inference cost, and being able to iterate fast, which is part of why open-sourcing made strategic sense: it commoditizes the layer that isn't our moat and lets the whole ecosystem do a lot of the hardening and tooling work for free.

Where I'm honest about the risks: the frontier is moving fast, and there's a real talent competition. Good researchers have a lot of options now, and a company this size has coordination overhead that a smaller lab doesn't. Also, open models give up some advantages. Once you release weights, your competitors can study them, and you can't easily monetize the model directly. So the open strategy only works if you're very confident the value accrues to the products, not the model.

The other thing I'd point out is that the interesting part of this field is shifting. Scaling pretraining is still important, but a lot of the gains now come from reasoning, from post-training, from models that can plan and search and use tools rather than just predict the next token. That's an area where the research side matters more than raw scale, and it's where I spend most of my own time. If that's where the next few years of progress come from, I'd say the playing field is more open than people assume, and Meta is in a reasonably good position.

So, overall: strong chances of staying near the frontier, I think a decent chance of winning on the dimension that matters for Meta's business, and genuine uncertainty about whether anyone, including us, has a durable lead at the very top. In this field a lead of a few months evaporates quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says any lead may last only a few months and questions whether anyone has a durable lead, but it does not state that there are no permanent winners.

astra-6.text:
I think Meta has a real chance, but I wouldn’t call the outcome predetermined. Building large models takes several things at once: compute, strong researchers, good engineering, and the ability to turn research into a reliable product. Meta has substantial strengths in those areas.

The harder question is how effectively those resources come together. Can a team run experiments quickly, learn from failures, and keep a clear direction as the technology changes? Having a lot of GPUs is valuable, but you still need to decide which experiments are worth running.

There’s also the question of what it means to win. Having the strongest model at a particular moment is one measure. Getting models into products people use, or building an ecosystem that other developers contribute to, is another. An open approach can be powerful there, because progress doesn’t have to come entirely from one company.

So I’m optimistic about Meta’s chances. But I’d judge them by sustained execution and how useful the models become, rather than by who leads on a benchmark at any one moment.

r001.rationale: The response says the outcome is not predetermined and that benchmark leadership at one moment is not the only measure. It does not clearly state that there are no permanent winners.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d look at it in terms of research talent, computing resources, and the ability to turn research into a product. Meta has strengths in all three, so I think it has a serious chance. But resources alone don’t guarantee that you’ll build the best model. Execution matters: how quickly a team can test ideas, learn from failed experiments, and decide what to scale.

There’s also a question of what it means to win. Having the strongest model at one moment is different from building a platform that developers and users keep coming back to. An open approach can help build that ecosystem, but the models still have to be capable and useful. So I’d see Meta as a strong contender, while being cautious about predicting a single winner.

r001.rationale: The response says Meta is a strong contender and cautions against predicting a single winner, but it does not state that there are no permanent winners in the competition.
